Photograph: Andrew Caballero-Reynolds/AFP via Getty Images Washington DC Trump arch will alter sightlines of many Washington DC landmarks, report says National Park Service, which backs the 250ft arch, says it is likely to disrupt historical significance of dozens of sites Associated Press Fri 28 Aug 2026 17.36 EDT Last modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 17.48 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A new National Park Service report backs Donald Trump ’s proposed arch, despite what it says are adverse effects to the sightlines of a host of landmarks in Washington, including the Washington Monument and the Lincoln and Jefferson memorials. The report released on Friday says the 250ft-tall (76-meter) memorial arch is likely to disrupt the historical significance of dozens of sites near its planned location adjacent to the Arlington Memorial Bridge. Many of Washington’s monuments, buildings and sites have been carefully planned over decades to reflect significant moments in the nation’s history and to evoke symbolism through sightlines that connect them to other sites. The arch will disturb the sightline between more Washington landmarks than anticipated, the report said. But the Park Service report says “the same characteristics that make Memorial Circle sensitive from a preservation perspective are also the characteristics that make it the historically appropriate location for the undertaking”. The project’s effects cannot be “fully avoided without either relocating the Arch away from the historically identified site or eliminating the principal commemorative feature, both of which would fail to meet the undertaking’s purpose and need”, the report said. “For this reason, alternative locations outside Memorial Circle are not reasonable avoidance alternatives,” the report said. The 133-page report by the park service supports Trump’s plans for the arch and could play an important role in bolstering the administration’s case in its fight against a legal challenge filed by three veterans and a group of historians. The proposed towering gilded arch, which last month received initial approval from a key federal commission, would affect the “integrity” of dozens of historic properties because it would change “character-defining visual and spatial relationships” among them. One of the most obvious elements the report cited is that the arch would break alignment among the Lincoln Memorial, Memorial Bridge and Arlington House, which was the Confederate general Robert E Lee’s home. That alignment was “intended to physically and symbolically unite North and South through a coordinated monumental composition extending across the Potomac River”, the report said. The Lincoln Memorial-Arlington House connection was one of dozens listed as being affected directly by the proposed structure. It added that the National Mall, the US Capitol, the Washington Monument, the Jefferson Memorial, the Georgetown Historic District, the Old Naval Observatory, the Francis Scott Key Bridge, the National Cathedral and other sites also would be affected. Nicolas Sansone, an attorney with Public Citizen Litigation Group, which is representing the plaintiffs, said the report “confirms what we’ve been saying all along: the project will have an enormous impact and transform that National Mall”. The report underscores the legal challengers’ claim that a project of this size and importance “is a decision for Congress to make” and should not be rushed through by executive decree, Sansone said. http://www.jpost.com/diaspora/article-91.text: After years of neglect, the historic synagogue in Trzebinia, Poland, has been acquired through an international initiative aimed at restoring it to its original purpose and returning it to the Jewish community.The plans include the restoration of the building, the establishment of a Jewish museum, and the creation of a hospitality center for visitors to the graves of revered rabbis and Hasidic leaders at the local Jewish cemetery.The historic synagogue, located in Poland's Silesian region, was returned to the Jewish people on Tuesday, after years of decay.The Jewish community of Katowice relinquished its right to reclaim the building, after which the municipality put it up for sale through a tender process.In response, a group of partners joined forces to prevent the property from being converted into a non-Jewish venue, and to ensure that it would be preserved as a site of Jewish historical significance.The acquisition of the synagogue was made possible through cooperation among three parties: the Israeli delegation, led by Meir Bulka, known as the “Grave Hunter,” who heads J-NERATIONS, an organization dedicated to preserving Jewish heritage in Europe; Jacek Purski, director of Auschwitz Research Center on Hate, Extremism and Radicalisation; and Marcin Majchrowicz, a businessman and philanthropist committed to preserving Jewish heritage in Poland's Silesian region.Community history The Jewish community in Trzebinia dates back to at least the 1500s, with a more prominent presence from the 1700s onward.An independent Jewish community was established in the city in 1815, growing to its peak in 1921 when Jews accounted for 23% of Trzebinia's population.Between the two World Wars, Trzebinia was home to four synagogues, a Talmud Torah, yeshivas, prayer houses, charitable institutions, and aid organizations.Among the prominent rabbinical figures who served in the city were Rabbi Dov Berish Weidenfeld, known as the Gaon of Tchebinas, as well as Rabbi Ben Zion Halberstam, the second Rebbe of Bobov.Adjacent to the synagogue is the Jewish cemetery, where rabbis and several spiritual leaders are buried.However, the Holocaust destroyed the vibrant Jewish community. Many members of the community were deported to concentration camps and ghettos, and numerous residents of the city were murdered at Auschwitz.The Jewish community's properties were destroyed, leaving the surviving synagogue as the only remaining testimony to the city's Jewish heritage.“The synagogue, located just a 40-minute drive from Kraków and now returned to the Jewish people, will soon become another destination for Jews visiting the region,” said Meir Bulka.“I am deeply moved that we have succeeded in preventing the desecration of Jewish religious heritage and in making a meaningful mark on the history of the Jewish people in Poland.""This is not merely about saving a synagogue; it is also about taking responsibility for preserving the memory of an entire community.”Polish synagogue restoration aims to preserve Jewish heritage for future generationsJacek Purski, director of Auschwitz Research Center on Hate, Extremism and Radicalization said that saving a synagogue is not purely about preserving a building, but about recognizing that Jewish life is "not only part of Poland's past, but also part of its present and future."Wherever possible, the partners said they will use historical documentation and archaeological evidence to recreate the site's appearance before the Holocaust.In the coming days, a foundation will be established in Poland to manage the restoration of the synagogue, and it will be possible to participate through donations and investments.
